stories.headline: Inside night Brewers booked World Series trip, ousted Dodgers
stories.summary: After dethroning the Dodgers, Milwaukee is celebrating its first Fall Classic berth since 1982 -- with its captain to thank for setting the tone.
stories.body:
LOS ANGELES -- In the midst of the crawl of revelers wandering around the Dodger Stadium field looking for people to hug late Thursday night, two old teammates came together in celebration.

It was eye-catching because both are former National League MVP winners with jet-black hair, one retired, one still very much in the thick of it. Both won those MVP trophies while wearing the uniform of a successful franchise with rabid fan support that is nonetheless one of the final five big league clubs without a championship.

That may soon change: The reason Ryan Braun and Christian Yelich embraced, posed for pictures together and generally beamed like happy children was that their Milwaukee Brewers had moved one step closer to removing their name from that final five list of nonchampions by clinching their first World Series trip in 44 years.

"They've brought me and all the former Brewers so much pride," Braun said. "We're all on group text and talking about this constantly. The way they play as a group, the belief they have in each other."

The Brewers had just knocked out the two-time champion Los Angeles Dodgers with alarming alacrity, shrugging off a four-run deficit created by a ballpark-shaking three-run homer off the previously dormant bat of Shohei Ohtani and rallying to win 6-4, completing a four-game sweep.

"This place is going crazy and all the momentum's swinging the other way," Yelich said. "And we're like, 'Hey, just stay together, guys. This is gonna be a great way to win it. Just chip away. This is gonna be a great story.'"

Yelich and his teammates were not wrong. For just the second time in 58 years of existence, 57 if you don't want to count their one-year expansion stint as the Seattle Pilots, the Milwaukee Brewers are headed to the World Series. The previous time, 1982, happened when the Brewers were still in the American League, so, by winning on Thursday, the Brewers removed their name from another list to avoid: Milwaukee was the only current NL franchise that had never won a flag in that circuit.

"Forty-four years of hope, 44 years of heartbreak, 44 years of believing that we would have our moment, and that moment has arrived," Braun said. "So I'm sure they're thrilled to have a team for the current generation of Brewers fans, because a lot of them probably weren't alive in '82."

It's a start.

"We have an unbelievable opportunity in front of us," Yelich said. "It's something that you dream about as a kid."

The Brewers have been knocking on this door for a decade. Braun was there at the start of it, before retiring in 2020, and Yelich has been there for nearly all of it, save for 2017, when Milwaukee began its streak of competitive seasons. Beginning with that campaign, Milwaukee has since played just two games after being eliminated from playoff contention. Thus, nearly every game Yelich has played in for Milwaukee -- 1,124, including the playoffs, has had something on the line.

But until Thursday, there had been a ceiling to Milwaukee's penchant for punching above its market weight -- the NLCS, with the Dodgers twice before serving as the brick wall into which the Brewers ran. That the Brewers finally crashed through and did it in Southern California, where Yelich and a number of his teammates are from, made it that much more gratifying.

"I don't know if you told me as a kid that this would be a thing that happened if I would believe you," Yelich said. "Which is pretty crazy. It's just an awesome moment and memory."

The pennant clincher came just 19 days after Yelich was named as the first team captain in Brewers history, an honor made tangible by the "C" that is now stitched onto his jersey. None of the greats in Brewers history -- Braun, Robin Yount, Paul Molitor, Cecil Cooper -- were so honored.

Yelich has become well-schooled in Brewers history, likely in part because it's hard to avoid in Milwaukee. The Brewers are pretty history-forward in the way they honor their greats in and around American Family Field. Yount, the Hall of Famer who rates pretty clearly as the best player in franchise history, is a frequent presence. When you walk into the Brewers' clubhouse, the first thing you see are a row of lockers with jerseys hanging in them -- Hank Aaron (who played his final two seasons with the Brewers after starring for the Milwaukee then Atlanta Braves), Yount, Molitor and Rollie Fingers among them.

"The team does a great job of bringing those guys back, giving them opportunities to come back, and when they do come back, they hang out in the clubhouse," NLCS MVP Jake Bauers said. "They talk to us. We get to hang out with them."

According to MLB.com, before Yelich accepted the captainship, he checked with Yount to get his blessing. That's how much respect he has for the Brewers who came before him. And while Yelich has forged a friendship with Yount over the years, one thing he has never asked about is that long-ago 1982 World Series.

Now might be a good time to inquire, especially since Yount hit .414 in that seven-game thriller against the St. Louis Cardinals.

"Hopefully he's around and we can have that conversation," Yelich said. "It would be awesome. He's a great guy. What an ambassador for the Brewers and just a pillar of the organization."

To pay a visit to American Family Field is to step into a ballpark that you'd never guess was the home of a team that was oh-for-history on the championship leaderboard. From the scores of pregame tailgaters who populate the sea of parking lots around the park, to the sight of Bernie the Brewer sliding down his chute after a Brewers home run, to the iconic sausage races, to the ritual of singing "Beer Barrel Polka" during the seventh-inning stretch, it is one of baseball's most distinct game-day experiences.

And even though Milwaukee is baseball's smallest market, the Brewers draw well, this season bringing in 2.788 million fans, which ranked 11th in the majors. That was more than the Mets and Angels, just to pick on two big-market franchises.

All of this is to suggest that this pennant, and the forthcoming shot at a title, is going to set the state of Wisconsin on its ear.

"We understand who we're playing for, what it means to the city," Yelich said. "They're going to be stoked, and we're so excited to get back to them. They've been unbelievable."

Yelich wasn't around for that 1982 pennant, of course, but he's been around for plenty of baseball success in Milwaukee. Since Yelich joined the team, the Brewers have made the playoffs in eight out of nine seasons. They've won six NL Central titles, including the past four. They have advanced to three National League Championship Series and, now, won a pennant. The Dodgers are the only NL team with more wins during that span.

Yet the reality of playing in Milwaukee means that even as Yelich has remained the face of the franchise and a fixture in the community, the team around him has iterated again and again, even as the wins continue to pile up. Thus it is on him to be the exemplar of what it means to be a Brewer.

"You can say you want to win, but you have to do the things and hold each other to the standard of being a really good team," Yelich said. "And we do a great job of that here."

The teammates have changed and the Brewers' style of play has evolved. Craig Counsell left for the rival Cubs, so Pat Murphy took over as manager. David Stearns earned widespread praise for his tenure as the Brewers' baseball operations honcho but is now with the Mets. Matt Arnold was promoted to replace Stearns following the 2022 season and, if anything, has upped the ante.

Yelich has been the one constant among the position players, with Brandon Woodruff filling a similar role for the pitchers. For teams looking to replicate what the Brewers have done, well, good luck because it's not a simple formula, but a complex and persistent iteration of top-to-bottom organizational best practices. But the value of having touchstone players like Yelich and Woodruff around is something that can be replicated because the benefits are tangible and intangible, and obvious.

"Yeli, he changed the culture here," Bauers said. "This is the better part of 10 years of work for him to really change this organization. So I don't know how he's feeling right now, but I'm sure it's pretty strong."

The break-through edition of the Brewers came together after years of good scouting, good development, good financial decisions and so much else. As the rosters evolved, getting better and better even though the previous versions were already good, incoming players had Yelich and Woodruff to turn to.

"They make the clubhouse go," All-Star second baseman Brice Turang said. "Their experiences and just teaching us some of their experiences or wanting us to be better in certain aspects of the game or teaching us the game, you learn. Even as you are in the big leagues, you're still learning all the time. Those guys are the guys to lean on to ask questions."

But as the Braun/Eric Thames upstarts of 2017 turned into the Yelich/Lorenzo Cain teams that featured the three-headed rotation monster of Woodruff, Corbin Burnes and Freddy Peralta, to the "jumbo infield" teams with Mike Moustakas, Jonathan Schoop and Travis Shaw, the Brewers were very gradually becoming what they are -- a team with a magical combination of youth, veteran presence, athleticism, skill, depth and loads of pitching.

One by one they joined Yelich in the clubhouse: Turang, Garrett Mitchell and Sal Frelick one year; Luis Lara and Cooper Pratt another. William Contreras. The sublime Jackson Chourio. Second-chance hitters like Bauers, Andrew Vaughn, Gary Sanchez. And those are just the position players.

"It's a special group," Yelich said. "Guys are willing to do whatever it takes to win. Like nobody nobody has an ego. Nobody cares who the guy is that gets it done. Nobody cares."

The talent was there in 2026, as it was in 2025, when the Brewers also fashioned baseball's best regular-season record. But something was different with this bunch. Somehow, with each roster change, the Brewers seemed to get closer, to operate more as one. A hive mentality emerged, an all-for-one ethos that was never mere rhetoric.

And Yelich, as the team's most recognizable player, meshed easily with the group, which game by game created something that has become recognizable as Brewers baseball. It's a vibe so apparent and infectious to anyone who has regularly watched the Brewers this season that the team's marketing arm has canned it into the slogan "Win Our Way."

"I couldn't be more proud of him," Braun said. "He has such a unique impact on this group of young guys, just with his ability to connect, his ability to be humble, to be himself, to come out and grind and compete every day, whether things are going great for him personally or not. He really helps us set the tone for the team."

As the Brewers were enjoying their best-ever regular season, winning a franchise-record 103 games, Yelich was having his worst. At 34, his OPS+ was a career-low 91 and he posted just 0.1 wins above replacement over 118 games.

Yelich has struggled with injuries and after his monster first two seasons in Milwaukee, he has operated on a lesser, but still admirable, performance tier. He's still young enough to bounce back from this season's struggles, but he's also at an age where it might simply be downhill from here.

With so many young standouts propelling the Brewers along, it might have been natural for Yelich to fade into the background, or to feel left out of the team's success. That wasn't the case, yet someone (identity unknown) had a notion and pinged Murphy with the idea of formalizing the essential role Yelich still played, numbers be damned, by naming him captain.

"All young people today coming into the game should be so lucky to be guided by a guy like this," Murphy said. "He doesn't bully them. He's not trying to browbeat them. He's not trying to convince them of everything. He's just living his life the way he lives his life, and he's welcoming. He's got so many great qualities, and he lives it."

Yelich isn't a shouter but instead remains incessantly friendly and accessible. He leads by example, in the clubhouse and beyond. This year he was the Brewers' nominee for the Roberto Clemente Award for the second time in four seasons. He's still a viable big league player, a regular on the National League champions. But he has become more than a good player. He has become a steward for the kind of baseball team, and organization, the Brewers want to be.

This is why after the Game 4 clincher, one in which Yelich went 0-for-4, he was one of the most sought out members of the Brewers. Everyone wanted to know what he was feeling, what it meant to him, as a player who's been knocking on the title door for nine years.

The door is now ajar. American Family Field will host its first World Series game ever on Oct. 23. And when Yelich is introduced before Game 1, the roar will be heard from Kenosha to the Wisconsin Dells. The former Marlin, by way of SoCal, is now the new Mr. Brewer.

"You understand that your performance as a team directly impacts the happiness of the people in the state," Yelich said. "You don't take that for granted. It's been awesome playing here. I've really loved it the last nine years and am looking forward to more."

ESPN reporter Vincent Goodwill wrote Friday about why the Detroit Pistons and big man Jalen Duren -- who engaged in a contract stalemate this offseason before Duren got a five-year, $200 million contract -- needed each other. The season ending Achilles injury to Ariel Hukporti has roster ramifications for the 76ers.

Doncic, who 'worked his butt off all summer,' lights up Kings
A lighter Luka Doncic scored an easy 21 first-half points in the Los Angeles Lakers' preseason opener over the Sacramento Kings on Monday night, needing only 16 minutes to sharpen up his game in a 127-103 blowout in Sacramento.
Doncic was listed at 244 pounds prior to the 2025-26 season. That dipped to 230 pounds entering training camp. The difference in physique from his heavier days is obvious.

"The guy worked his butt off all summer staying in shape and actually ran this summer," coach JJ Redick said. "He actually did like sprints and stuff. Came into camp in fantastic shape."

The Lakers were without Austin Reaves and Walker Kessler in the preseason opener. Reaves tweaked his ankle recently, and Kessler jammed a finger on the backboard. Both are listed as day-to-day. Without either, the Lakers still rolled through the Kings. Doncic scored all 21 of his points in a 73-point Lakers first half, resting while the backups finished the job. He made three 3s, four shots in the paint and got to the line for nine free throws.

"For someone who normally plays a ton of live basketball [in the summer], he didn't do as much of that by design," Redick said. "We've seen him literally every day in camp incrementally get more and more in rhythm."

Doncic badly strained his hamstring in early April and missed the entire Lakers playoff run while rehabbing the injury. He said he felt "great" against the Kings but downplayed any larger changes to his training regimen.

"I feel probably a little more rested," Doncic said. "I didn't play [on the Slovenian] national team." -- Anthony Slater

Golden State could increase its projection to $55 million if center Kristaps Porzingis is waived in the offseason. Porzingis' $20 million salary for next season is guaranteed for $3 million.

For Golden State to have ample room, forwards Draymond Green and Jimmy Butler III would need to sign elsewhere or at a significantly lesser salary. They will be free agents next summer.

Both salary projections include the $17 million free agent hold of guard Brandin Podziemski. The 2023 first-round pick is eligible until Oct. 19 to extend his contract. -- Bobby Marks

Hornets star Knueppel sidelined by hamstring injury

James: Maxey, Embiid were factors in joining 76ers
LeBron James said his longstanding friendship with All-Star Tyrese Maxey and a desire to help Joel Embiid win his first NBA title played significant roles in his decision to sign a two-year, $8 million contract with the Philadelphia 76ers in July.

"[Embiid has] done everything in our league, and the only thing he has not done is win a championship. And I want to try to help him get that first one," James said. "He has a city on his back. He's been 'The Process' for 10 years, 12 years, however long he's been there. But I think it's time we even get you deeper into the process. And I hope that I can be, kind of, that final little piece that can help him get over the hump."

stories.headline: Brady Tkachuk third in NHL history with back-to-back natural hat tricks
stories.summary: Brady Tkachuk became the second player in almost 40 years and the third player in NHL history to score a natural hat trick -- three consecutive goals without another player from either team scoring -- in back-to-back games.
stories.body:
SUNRISE, Fla. -- With one swipe of his stick in overtime, Brady Tkachuk gave Florida a victory, joined a very small group of Panthers and claimed family bragging rights.

Welcome to Florida, Brady.

Tkachuk had his second consecutive hat trick, joining only Pavel Bure and Noel Acciari on the list of Panthers players with three goals in back-to-back games, to carry Florida to a come-from-behind, 3-2 victory over the Vancouver Canucks on Thursday night.

"It's pretty cool, but I know what my goal is being here and that's to be part of something special," Tkachuk said. "It's not about the individual stuff. Yeah, it's great, but there are bigger goals out there."

He is the first member of his star-studded family to have six goals in a two-game span. His father, Hall of Famer Keith Tkachuk, had five goals in a two-game stretch on three occasions. His brother, fellow Florida forward Matthew Tkachuk, has never had more than four goals in two games.

Brady Tkachuk became the second player in almost 40 years and the third player in NHL history to score a natural hat trick -- three consecutive goals without another player from either team scoring -- in back-to-back games. Petri Skriko did it for the Vancouver Canucks in 1986, and Cy Denneny did it in 1923 with the original Ottawa Senators.

"Today was pretty special," Brady Tkachuk said.

The last NHL player with back-to-back hat tricks in regular-season play was Toronto's Auston Matthews in February 2024. Dallas' Mikko Rantanen pulled it off during the 2025 Stanley Cup playoffs.

"Those guys who have had great success in their career in big moments, they can feel it," Panthers coach Paul Maurice said. "They want it."

Tkachuk's first three-goal game of the season was Tuesday in Florida's 7-3 win at Columbus, when he netted them all in a span of 8:03 of the second period. On Thursday, it was another quick blitz that got it done.

His goal with 8:49 left in regulation got Florida to 2-1. He tied it with 12.8 seconds left in regulation, almost won it with a drive five seconds into overtime then got the winner 2:23 into the extra session. Add it up, and the hat trick Thursday came in a span of 11:12.

"Awesome. Awesome. He's a true gamer," said Panthers defenseman Seth Jones, who assisted two of Tkachuk's goals on Thursday and one of his scores Tuesday. "He's obviously scoring right now, but he impacts the game in so many ways -- his physicality and his tenacity."

Brady Tkachuk came to Florida this offseason in a trade from Ottawa. He spent eight years with the Senators, who sent him to the Panthers for four draft picks. Social media was ablaze with criticism after the first six games of Florida's season, with Tkachuk managing only one point and zero goals.

A couple of hat tricks have made his numbers look a whole lot better.

"I don't think anybody puts more pressure on myself than me," Tkachuk said. "It wasn't the start that I wanted or envisioned, but with this group, everybody's there for one another. Just had to stick with it and knew it was eventually going to come. Didn't expect what followed, but every day has just been a blast being here, being with this group. It's truly a special group."

stories.headline: Harry Kane has talent for NFL - Jags kicker Cam Little
stories.summary: Cam Little is confident Harry Kane has the skill to become an NFL kicker.
stories.body:
LONDON -- Cam Little is confident Harry Kane has the skill to become an NFL kicker.

But the hard part for Kane, the Jacksonville Jaguars kicker said, would be shifting from star striker to bit player.

"I think the transition from soccer to football is so much more cultural than like the actual skill," Little said.

The England captain and Bayern Munich forward has mused over the years about one day kicking in the NFL. He recently floated the idea of combining his NFL goal with also joining an MLS team.

Who better to weigh in than Little? The soccer player-turned kicker, who remains a diehard Manchester United fan, booted a 57-yard field goal as time expired for the Jags to defeat the Philadelphia Eagles 19-17 last Sunday at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. He also holds the record for longest NFL field goal -- 68 yards.

"It's just so different," Little told The Associated Press of moving from being involved in a game for 90 minutes to being a kicker "sitting there on the sidelines the whole game.

"You're not going to get on the ball, and you don't have the same moxie, I guess, because he is a star striker for the team. So that moxie is just kind of put to the side. You've got to let everyone else do the big man's job, and then you're out there just to back everyone up basically."

As far as Kane's ability, "he's probably talented enough to do it ... His technique in soccer is so good. But it's just such a different mental, I'd say, challenge than soccer.

"It'd be like him taking five set pieces a day. And he's got to deliver on all five set pieces, or you didn't do your job for the day," Little said Thursday after practice at the team's accommodations north of London in Watford.

"So, it's just a lot different, but I don't think he doesn't have the talent level for it. I think he probably has the skill to do it."

Little and the Jaguars remained in London this week ahead of the game against the Houston Texans on Sunday at Wembley Stadium.

Little, a sixth-round draft pick from Arkansas in 2024, had missed an extra-point attempt -- after a high snap from fill-in long snapper DaVon Hamilton -- late in the fourth quarter against the Eagles. The miss had looked crucial because Philadelphia then took a 17-16 lead with just 8 seconds left -- before the improbable ending on Little's heroics.

"Missing a set piece or missing a wide-open goal, you see a lot of strikers do that, and they'll come back and put the game away," Little said at his post-game news conference while wearing a Man United jersey. "I've got to have short-term memory and be at my best when the best is required."

Little told AP that he'd be attending Fulham's home game against Hull at Craven Cottage on Saturday. Jaguars owner Shad Khan also owns the Premier League club.

Little, an Oklahoma native, played as a midfielder before switching to American football in high school. England and United great Wayne Rooney was his favorite player.

"Maybe one day I'll get to meet him or do a jersey swap with him. That's my goal," he said. "I've never been to Manchester. Only London, but I'm hoping to make it there this offseason."

stories.headline: Shakhtar's Champions League win vs. AEK was more than just a game
stories.summary: Shakhtar Donetsk haven't played at home since 2014 due to the war, and this season, their Champions League home games are at Chelsea's Stamford Bridge. Wednesday's win was a reminder of how absurd their situation is.
stories.body:
LONDON -- Take a step back and revel in the absurdity for a minute. Shakhtar Donetsk, a Ukrainian team from the Russian-speaking part of the country, are playing a Greek team, AEK Athens, in London, at Chelsea's Stamford Bridge. Technically, it's a "home game," but that concept has become rather meaningless.

Shakhtar haven't played at their home, the Donbas Arena, since May 2014, some 650 weeks ago. They turn up wherever someone will host them: Odessa, Kyiv, Kharkiv and Lviv for Ukrainian league games; Warsaw, Hamburg, Gelsenkirchen, Krakow, Ljubljana and now London for matches in European competition. Why? Because their opponents can't (or won't) travel to Ukraine, where none of the civilian airports are open, air raid sirens go off a dozen times a day, and where drones and bombs can't be trusted to distinguish between a military captain and the captain of a soccer team.

It's pretty obvious that in those circumstances, you're more than a club -- you're a symbol of defiance, an attempt to maintain some sort of normality in the face of a war that has taken more than half a million lives and displaced tens of millions more.

"We are playing for people from Ukraine all over the world," sporting director Dario Srna said. "Everywhere we've gone, they've come [to see us]. We represent Ukraine in the center of the world: we're not just playing for us. [We are] a Ukrainian team, we are not just Shakhtar."

But, of course, nothing is normal. Everything is messed up, and their mere presence in the Champions League constitutes a political dimension.

Wednesday night, Shakhtar were at Stamford Bridge, the home of Chelsea. Resourceful as ever, street vendors outside the ground hawked their off-brand scarves, except rather than "Cole Palmer," "João Pedro" and "John Terry," the names read "Pedrinho," "[Mykola] Matviyenko" and "[Valeriy] Bondar." Watching over them was a life-size cardboard cutout of Dwayne Johnson, aka The Rock, only his face was replaced by that of Ukrainian President Vladimir Zelenskyy.

Inside, visiting AEK fans -- who turned the Shed End into a two-tier wall of tifo, flags and noise -- outsing, if not outnumber, the "home" support.

Because yes, this is Shakhtar's home for the Champions League this season, a move made possible by the London club's failure to qualify for European competitions (and, probably, a need to rake in some extra rent on those empty weeknights). Ironically, Chelsea's previous owner, Roman Abramovich, was forced by the U.K. government to sell the club after the invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, because of his ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Abramovich holds passports from Portugal, Israel and Russia. His yachts are moored in Turkey.

Abramovich, whose mother is Ukrainian, is a complicated figure. So is Shakhtar's version of Abramovich, Rinat Akhmetov.

An ethnic Russian, but Donetsk-born and bred, Akhmetov's huge wealth from mining and energy bankrolled the club's rise to prominence prewar -- lest we forget, the likes of Willian and Fernandinho, Henrikh Mkiytaryan and Douglas Costa are all Shakhtar alums -- and keeps it alive and very much kicking today. Forbes estimates his wealth at nearly $8 billion and like most folks of that ilk, Akhmetov could easily have made different choices, decamping abroad. When the war broke out, he chose to stay, and that was not something to take for granted, given that he had previously clashed with Zelenskyy and, in the 2000s, served in parliament in the party of former pro-Russian Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovych, whom he also backed financially.

Akhmetov broke with Yanukovych in 2014 and while his pro-Ukrainian words today are loud, his actions -- from staying in the country to tirelessly campaigning to his efforts with Shakhtar -- speak even louder.

"He can't leave Ukraine, not after seeing what he has seen," Srna says of Akhmetov. "It's impossible. He's devoted himself to this, helping the economy, helping the people. All while sleeping each night under bombs."

Many Ukrainians have no choice, which makes the actions of those who could be elsewhere all the more remarkable. It takes an unconventional type of person.

Most of Shakhtar's players are Brazilian -- lured by money, sure, but also the opportunity to showcase their talent. The coach, former Atletico Madrid and Barcelona standout Arda Turan, is Turkish. Even if you don't remember what he was like as a player, watching him prowl the technical area during the AEK game, fists clenched and eyes wild, you come to understand how this is the same guy who once got into an altercation with a pop star in an Istanbul hospital.

Srna himself is Croatian, but has been at the club -- first as a player then as sporting director -- for 23 years. He too could have left umpteen times and, in fact, he says he even turned down the chance to take over Barcelona's recruitment a decade ago.

"Ukraine and Shakhtar are in my blood," he says. "If I leave now, I couldn't live with myself."

In some ways, Srna has been here before. He was eight years old when civil war broke out in the former Yugoslavia in March 1991. The conflict that would rage for 4½ years, ripped apart communities along ethnic lines. Neighbors took up arms against neighbors. His own father woke up every day supplying baked goods for the military. If you've seen the ESPN 30 for 30 documentary "Once Brothers" about the relationship between Drazen Petrovic and Vlade Divac, well ... he lived it. Twice. Maybe that's why he soldiers on, numb to what he is experiencing.

"I have this feeling inside myself," he says. "It's a feeling I felt before [as a child experiencing war in Croatia]. But when you feel that pain and it comes back to you again, well, you're not going to have the same pain twice. I know this pain. I know this feeling ..."

Srna trails off as he searches for the right words of history -- the worst parts -- repeating itself with him in the middle of it. But then he flickers back with righteous anger.

"This is unbelievable, I can't explain it," he says. "Four-and-a-half years [this war has continued]. Bombing each other, destroying everything ... for what? For f---ing what? People die, families are destroyed, children are traumatized and grow up with psychological problems ..."

On this Wednesday night, even as Shakhtar emerge as 3-1 victors over AEK, you're reminded once again of the difficulties. The team were up at 6 a.m. on Thursday to catch a 10 o'clock flight on a plane they chartered from a budget airline taking them back to Rzeszow in Poland. They'll then board a bus back across the border into Ukraine, arriving -- best-case scenario -- at 9 p.m. local time. All this not knowing whether they'll have power and heat when they arrive, or whether they'll be making regular trips into the air raid shelter.

You want to end on a note of hope. Srna does his best to offer it, but he clearly isn't going to lie to you or to himself.

"We [Croatians] have more or less an OK relationship now with Serbia," he says. "Time [30 years have passed] is helping, generations change, it's different people. We take a step back and understand what was good, what was not good. We can't say all Serbian people are bad ... But in this moment, it's not possible to be friends with a Russian person. In time, maybe a few years, maybe many years, I don't know ... right now though, it's impossible."

Certainly more impossible than a club without a home in a country at war defying logic and competing in the Champions League against the likes of Real Madrid, who visit Stamford Bridge on Jan. 27.

One of the side effects of war is the normalization of the horrific and the absurd. Shakhtar's plight has, by necessity, normalized the absurd, in an effort to stave off the horrific.

stories.headline: Ranking Angel Reese and the top 15 players in the WNBA Finals
stories.summary: Which Valkyries and Dream players have played the best so far in the postseason heading into the WNBA Finals?
stories.byline: Michael Voepel and Alexa Philippou and Kendra Andrews and Kareem Copeland
stories.body:
Two teams. One title on the line.

The WNBA Finals open Saturday (3:30 p.m. ET) as the No. 2 seed Golden State Valkyries and No. 4 Atlanta Dream square off in a best-of-seven series. Both are seeking their first championship. Which players are most likely to help them finish on top?

ESPN has ranked the top players throughout the 2026 season. Now we update our list one final time to reflect the 15 players who have performed the best in the playoffs.

Rotations get shorter in the postseason, but with their incredible depth, it's likely no surprise the Valkyries added one more player in our rankings. But with three All-Stars on their roster, it's perhaps also no shock that the Dream dominated the top, with three of the first four players.

The rankings come with one asterisk: Dream guard Allisha Gray, when healthy, is easily one of the WNBA's best. But she sustained a hand injury in the first game of the semifinals and hasn't played since.

Gray made the cut after she said Thursday she was optimistic about playing in Game 1 at Chase Center in San Francisco.

Here are the best 15 players in the postseason, as ranked by Michael Voepel, Alexa Philippou, Kendra Andrews and Kareem Copeland.

1. Angel Reese, Atlanta Dream
Forward | 6-foot-3

Playoff stats: 18.0 PPG, 8.4 RPG, 2.0 APG

The 2024 No. 7 draft pick is playing the best ball of her career and was recently named the league's Defensive Player of the Year. In her first postseason, Reese is averaging 18.0 points, 8.4 rebounds, 2.2 blocks, 2.0 assists and 1.6 steals. The scoring and blocks have both increased and she's shooting 38.5% from beyond the arc. Reese's impact on both ends of the court is, arguably, the biggest reason the Dream are in the Finals for the first time since 2013. -- Copeland

2. Gabby Williams, Golden State Valkyries
Forward | 5-foot-11

Playoff stats: 22.7 PPG, 4.8 RPG, 4.0 APG

Williams' breakout offensive season has continued in the playoffs. She is the highest scorer remaining in the Finals, averaging nearly 23 points, eight more than her regular-season average. She is shooting 40.5% from 3 on 2.8 attempts (fourth in the playoffs, and the most among players in the Finals). After finishing second in Defensive Player of the Year voting, Williams' two-way play has the Valkyries in the Finals and within striking distance of winning a title. -- Andrews

3. Rhyne Howard, Atlanta Dream
Guard | 6-foot-2

Playoff stats: 19.2 PPG, 4.2 RPG, 3.4 APG

Howard has had an up-and-down playoffs. She didn't make more than a third of her shots from the field in any of the semifinal games, though she went 4-for-10 from deep in Game 3 to help the Dream close out the series. She still excels with her versatility, whether she's making 3s, getting downhill and drawing contact, facilitating for teammates or wreaking havoc on defense. -- Philippou

4. Jordin Canada, Atlanta Dream
Guard | 5-foot-6

Playoff stats: 19.2 PPG, 3.8 RPG, 8.8 APG

Canada, the No. 5 pick in the 2018 draft, won two WNBA titles in 2018 and 2020 with Seattle. She was a backup to Sue Bird then and didn't start any of those postseason games but played valuable minutes. Now she is in the driver's seat during these playoffs, averaging almost seven points more in the Dream's five postseason games than she did in the regular season. She has also been a defensive catalyst, averaging 2.2 steals. At 31, Canada is playing her best basketball at the best time. -- Voepel

5. Veronica Burton, Golden State Valkyries
Guard | 5-foot-9

Playoff stats: 9.5 PPG, 4.0 RPG, 4.0 APG

Burton hasn't had the most consistent postseason run, but she has delivered some of the Valkyries' biggest shots when they've needed a bucket the most. After not scoring late into Game 2 against Las Vegas in the semifinals, Burton hit a 28-foot 3-pointer to give the Valkyries the lead with about 90 seconds left. In the first round, she also hit a dagger shot against Dallas to help come back from being down 16 to win the game -- and the series. -- Andrews

6. Allisha Gray, Atlanta Dream
Guard | 6-foot

Playoff stats: 17.0 PPG, 1.7 RPG, 2.0 SPG (three games)

Gray was the Dream's top scorer in the regular season and in the first round of the playoffs but is lower on this list than she'd typically be because of her limited availability in the postseason. She went down with an injury to her left (shooting) hand in the first half of Game 1 of the semifinals and hasn't played since, though she was questionable going into Game 3. Gray disclosed this week that she underwent a minor procedure for the injury and is still considered day-to-day. She told reporters Thursday she was hopeful about her availability for Game 1. -- Philippou

7. Tiffany Hayes, Golden State Valkyries
Guard | 5-foot-10

Playoff stats: 13.3 PPG, 2.8 RPG, 2.3 APG

The 14-year veteran has provided the offensive punch off the bench that the Valkyries have needed. Her 13.3 points per game during the playoffs, after a 9.0 regular-season average, ranks No. 3 on a team known more for defense than offense. She dropped 21 points in a Game 1 win over the Wings in the opening round, then went for 18 in the Game 3 series clincher. Hayes scored 21 points in less than 17 minutes in the Game 2 semifinal against Las Vegas. -- Copeland

8. Kiah Stokes, Golden State Valkyries
Center | 6-foot-3

Playoff stats: 3.2 PPG, 9.5 RPG, 2.0 BPG

One of the ultimate "stats don't define her" players, Stokes' value is in how well she fills the exact role she's asked to play. Still, one stat stands out: She has averaged almost four more rebounds in the playoffs than the regular season. She is a textbook solid defender who benefited from guarding A'ja Wilson in practice during their five years in Las Vegas. While there, Stokes won three WNBA championships. During the Valkyries' semifinal series sweep, Stokes used her experience to make things tough for Wilson and the Aces. Now she will try to do the same against Reese and the Dream. -- Voepel

9. DeWanna Bonner, Atlanta Dream
Forward | 6-foot-4

Playoff stats: 13.2 PPG, 6.4 RPG, 1.6 APG

After starting the season in Phoenix, Bonner joined the Dream with five games left in the regular season and has been a seamless fit so far for Atlanta, which desperately needed more depth entering the postseason. The two-time WNBA champion has slotted into the starting five since Gray went down with her injury and has hit double figures in four of Atlanta's five playoff games, including a 23-point outing in Game 1 of the semifinals. -- Philippou

10. Kayla Thornton, Golden State Valkyries
Forward | 6-foot-1

Playoff stats: 10.8 PPG, 5.7 RPG, 0.5 APG

Known for her 3-point shooting and perimeter defense abilities, Thornton has raised her game in the postseason. She's averaging more than three points more per game than the regular season and her 3-point percentage has climbed from 34.7% to 42.3%. This is the most productive the 11-year veteran has ever been in the postseason, scoring 16 points with three triples in Game 2 against the Aces and putting up 18 points and nine rebounds in the Game 3 closeout to advance to the Finals. Those points were the second- and third-most of her playoff career. Four of Thornton's five double-digit playoff scoring games have come in 2026. -- Copeland

11. Cecilia Zandalasini, Golden State Valkyries
Forward | 6-foot-2

Playoff stats: 8.5 PPG, 2.2 RPG, 1.2 SPG

Zandalasini's performance in Game 1 of the first round against the Wings illustrates how important she is for Golden State and how dangerous she can be as a floor spacer. She scored 22 points in that game, knocking down 4 of 5 3-point attempts. This is what she does best: hit important shots and provide momentum-shifting stretches. She is shooting 42.1% from beyond the arc in the postseason, while also playing an important role as a rebounder. -- Andrews

12. Naz Hillmon, Atlanta Dream
Forward | 6-foot-2

Playoff stats: 5.2 PPG, 4.4 RPG, 2.6 APG

Hillmon's scoring might be a bit down from her regular-season numbers (9.1 PPG) but she has still made an impact for the Dream in the playoffs -- especially defensively, where she made life difficult for Breanna Stewart in the semifinals. -- Philippou

13. Kaila Charles, Golden State Valkyries
Guard/forward | 6-foot-1

Playoff stats: 6.3 PPG, 4.2 RPG, 0.8 APG

Golden State is the fifth WNBA team Charles -- a second-round draft pick in 2020 -- has played for, and it has been the best fit for her. Charles has played in every game this season, and her stats are almost identical between the regular season and postseason. She personifies the team chemistry and willingness to play however many minutes she is given with the same energy. It's part of what has made her a fan favorite in the Bay Area. -- Voepel

14. Kaitlyn Chen, Golden State Valkyries
Guard | 5-foot-9

Playoff stats: 6.0 PPG, 1.5 RPG, 1.2 APG

Chen's minutes have dipped in the playoffs, but she has made the most of limited opportunities. Getting 17 minutes in Game 1 against the Wings, she scored eight points with two rebounds, two assists and two 3-pointers. In Game 1 against the Aces, Chen scored a playoff career-high 11 points in 22 minutes, also grabbing three rebounds. Starring in her reserve role, the second-year guard has been the loudest and most animated supporter of her teammates while on the bench. -- Copeland

15. Isobel Borlase, Atlanta Dream
Guard | 5-foot-11

Playoff stats: 5.6 PPG, 1.8 RPG, 0.8 APG

The Dream drafted "Izzy" in the second round in 2024 out of Australia at age 19, knowing she would need some time to develop before joining the WNBA. Atlanta's plans for her have worked out. The rookie, who turned 22 in September, appeared in all 44 games in the regular season, averaging 4.8 points and 13.0 minutes. In the postseason, she has played a similar role, giving the Dream important minutes off the bench, especially with fellow guard Gray having sat out most of the semifinals. -- Voepel

stories.body:
The 2026 rule changes threw Formula 1 into a new era of challenges and uncertainty, but the real moments of unpredictability are still to come.

Most drivers secured short-term deals to survive the regulation shift, leaving the grid wide open for the following year. With only a handful of drivers locked into long-term contracts almost every seat on the grid is up for grabs.

Here is our early look at what the future holds for the current Formula 1 lineup.

McLaren

Lando Norris - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2030

Prior to the start of the 2024 F1 season Norris agreed to an "extended multi-year contract beyond 2025."

The reigning champion has now signed a new contract with McLaren until at least 2030. The deal, which includes one of his title-winning Formula 1 cars as a gift from the team, also has the option of a "multi-year" extension beyond 2030.

Oscar Piastri - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2026

Ahead of the first race of the 2025 F1 season Piastri also signed a multi-year contract extension. His previous deal already ran until the end of 2026, and his latest agreement is likely to keep him at McLaren until at least the end of 2028 -- though speculation continues to rumble on about his long-term future.

Ferrari

Lewis Hamilton - 2027

While an exact end date of Hamilton's contract -- signed after completing one of the biggest driver moves in F1 history -- was never officially communicated, Hamilton admitted earlier this year that he still had a contract in place for 2027. That means he got at least a three-year deal at Ferrari, something he had also been seeking at Mercedes.

Amid retirement rumours, Hamilton has also crushed speculation and assured fans that he wasn't going anywhere just yet.

He said: "There's a lot of people that are trying to retire me, and that's not even in my thoughts. I'm already thinking of what will be next, and planning for, like, the next five years. But I still plan to be here for some time."

Charles Leclerc - 2028

Leclerc, who first joined Ferrari in 2019, signed another multi-year extension ahead of the 2026 Monaco Grand Prix.

The team did not publicly reveal an exact expiry date, but the new agreement is understood to take Leclerc to 2028 and potentially beyond, giving Ferrari long-term security over one side of its driver lineup.

Red Bull

Max Verstappen - 2030

Red Bull confirmed in 2022 that four-time world champion Verstappen would remain with the team until the end of 2028 in one of the longest deals on the F1 grid.

Sources told ESPN that performance-related clauses in Verstappen's contract could allow him to leave early, but the Dutchman has now signed a new contract extension with Red Bull until 2030 ahead of the Dutch Grand Prix.

Isack Hadjar - 2027

Isack Hadjar was promoted from Racing Bulls to partner Verstappen for the 2026 season after an impressive rookie campaign. He has now signed a contract extension with Red Bull, securing his seat for the 2027 season.

Mercedes

George Russell - beyond 2026

Russell agreed a new deal with Mercedes ahead of the 2026 season following lengthy negotiations with team principal Toto Wolff.

Although the agreement was initially confirmed as taking him through at least 2026, Russell has since described it as a multi-year deal and said he will fulfill the performance clauses in his contract to stay at Mercedes next year.

Kimi Antonelli - TBC

Mercedes' Antonelli has only been given one-year contracts since his debut, but given his form this season there's no way he'll be leaving the Silver Arrows. Right?

No official announcements have been made yet, but Antonelli could be celebrating both a maiden title and a bumper new deal this year.

Aston Martin

Fernando Alonso - TBC

Alonso's current Aston Martin deal runs until the end of the 2026 season, and he said a decision on his future will come later in the year. At 45 years old, the decision is likely to be between continuing with an underperforming Aston Martin team, or calling time on his F1 career once and for all.

Lance Stroll - TBC

Stroll signed a contract extension in 2024 which kept him with Aston Martin for 2025 "and beyond," but no specific end date was announced. Part of that ambiguity, of course, is because he's the son of team owner Lawrence Stroll.

He remains with the team for 2026, although his position for 2027 has not formally been confirmed.

Alpine

Pierre Gasly - 2028

Gasly is one of the drivers whose future is already settled -- the Frenchman signed a new multi-year agreement with Alpine in 2025 which keeps him locked in at the team until at least the end of the 2028 season.

Franco Colapinto - 2027

Colapinto retained his Alpine seat alongside Gasly for 2026 after taking over from Jack Doohan during the previous season. He has now signed a new contract with the team, meaning the Argentinian will continue with Alpine for the 2027 season.

Haas

Rafael Câmara - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2027

F2 star Câmara will replace Esteban Ocon for the 2027 season on a multi-year agreement. The reigning Formula 3 champion and current Formula 2 leader will make his debut in F1 and will partner fellow Ferrari Driver Academy member Oliver Bearman.

Oliver Bearman - TBC

Bearman joined Haas on a multi-year deal when he became a full-time F1 driver in 2025. The exact duration of Bearman's contract has not been made public, leaving his 2027 status uncertain for now.

However, sources with good knowledge of the team's thinking have told ESPN that Bearman is almost certain to stay with the team in 2027 unless a Ferrari seat opens up, then the Englishman remains effectively loaned to Haas.

Racing Bulls

Liam Lawson - TBC

Lawson remained with Racing Bulls for 2026 after rebuilding his season following a short-lived promotion to Red Bull the previous year.

His seat is only confirmed for the current season, meaning the New Zealander will again have to prove his case if he is to stay within the Red Bull set-up in 2027.

Arvid Lindblad - TBC

Lindblad became the latest Red Bull junior to make the jump to Formula 1 when he was handed a Racing Bulls seat for 2026.

The rookie is currently only confirmed for this season and the team have played down speculation over their driver lineup for 2027. You'd be shocked to see him go anywhere, though.

Williams

Carlos Sainz - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2026

Sainz originally joined Williams on a deal covering the 2025 and 2026 seasons, with "options to extend" his stay beyond that. He has recently spoken about wanting to make the Williams project work, leading to him signing a new multi-year extension with the team.

Alex Albon - 2027

Albon signed a new one-year contract with Williams during the summer break, tying him down for the 2027 season. The short-term deal is interesting, given Albon's last contract -- signed in 2024 -- was for multiple years. Keeping those options open?

Audi

Nico Hulkenberg - TBC

Hulkenberg joined Sauber ahead of its transformation into the Audi team on a multi-year contract in 2025.

There are believed to be options in his deal which could allow him to remain with Audi beyond 2026, but an exact end date has not been announced.

Gabriel Bortoleto - TBC

Bortoleto joined Hulkenberg at Sauber before the team's transition to Audi and also signed a multi-year deal.

The Brazilian is contracted through at least the end of 2026, but his place for 2027 has not yet been officially confirmed.

Cadillac

Sergio Perez - 2027

Perez returned to the Formula 1 grid with Cadillac for the team's debut season in 2026 after spending a year away from racing.

The Mexican joined on a multi-year agreement understood to be on similar terms to teammate Valtteri Bottas, putting him in line to remain with Cadillac for 2027.

Valtteri Bottas - 2027

Bottas also returned to a full-time race seat with Cadillac after spending 2025 as Mercedes' reserve driver.

The Finn signed a multi-year deal which runs until at least the end of 2027, giving the new team one of the few already settled driver pairings heading into next season.

stories.headline: UFC champ Alexander Volkanovski proposes 'send-off' superbout vs. Justin Gaethje
stories.summary: UFC featherweight champion Alexander Volkanovski is calling for a "send-off" superfight against lightweight champion Justin Gaethje.
stories.body:
UFC featherweight champion Alexander Volkanovski has proposed a "send-off" superfight between himself and lightweight champion Justin Gaethje.

Volkanovski (28-4) is scheduled to defend his 145-pound title against Movsar Evloev (20-0) at UFC 333 on Oct. 24 in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. Arguably the greatest featherweight of all time, Volkanovski has acknowledged he is approaching the end of his career at 38 years old. Gaethje, 37, has acknowledged the same since he claimed the UFC's 155-pound title for the first time in June.

With both champions seemingly near the end of their time in the Octagon, Volkanovski has suggested a winner-take-all scenario in 2027.

"Imagine that, do it as a send-off," Volkanovski told the "Who Da Fook Are These Guys?" podcast. "Gaethje, Volk. I think he's said that he maybe has one more. That could be a superfight. Let's do a superfight with the lightweight title on the line. We can both see everyone off with a crazy superfight. That could be really good."

Volkanovski, of Australia, has already tried to capture the lightweight title. He famously challenged then-lightweight champion Islam Makhachev twice in a 10-month span in 2023. He suffered a razor-close decision loss to Makhachev in their first meeting in February then lost by first-round knockout in an October rematch that was scheduled on short notice.

Gaethje (28-5) has not even guaranteed whether he will fight again or retire off his historic win at the White House in June, but he has stated that he believes his next challenger would be lightweight contender Arman Tsarukyan. Volkanovski appears to be throwing his name into the mix in the hope of changing those plans.

"He's said, 'What's the point of doing rematches,'" Volkanovski said. "Let's do a superfight then [retire] straight away after, let the divisions sort themselves out. The UFC would be happy for that. Let's make it happen."

stories.headline: Judge sides with NRL over NZ Rugby on Chiefs name
stories.summary: Rugby league has struck the first blow in the Chief name wars, with New Zealand Rugby's urgent injunction denied ahead of the new PNG NRL club's jersey reveal.
stories.body:
New Zealand's High Court has knocked back an application for an interim injunction on the PNG Chiefs NRL franchise using its name in the country.

New Zealand Rugby (NZR) had rushed to court ahead of the PNG team's logo and jersey reveal in Port Moresby next week.

The organisation claimed use of the Chiefs name, also the name of the long-standing Super Rugby Pacific outfit, would cause confusion and damage to the brand value.

But a judge at Friday's two-hour Wellington hearing turned down the application after hearing an injunction could harm the NRL expansion outfit's efforts to attract players ahead of a 2028 debut.

The dispute remains though, with the application for a final injunction still before the court and legal action in Australia a consideration.

ARLC executive chairman Peter V'landys last week labelled NZR's action one of "mind-blowing hypocrisy", using the example of the Auckland Blues' arrival decades after the NSW Blues "had been the Blues".

"Today's decision is not a judgement on the strength of our case, and the matter will still be heard in full," NZR boss Steve Lancaster said.

"As the trademark holder, our responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand hasn't changed. We remain open to working with the ARLC on a solution."

NZR's lawyer Earl Gray argued on Friday that the PNG Chiefs' use of 'PNG Chiefs' and 'Chiefs' interchangeably created confusion for fans of both codes and that, with no clear distinction between the two, it would strip the rugby Chiefs' brand exclusivity.

He said NZR had trademark protections for the Chiefs in New Zealand that the NRL had not acknowledged.

ARLC laywer Clive Elliot argued that the request for an urgent injunction, about a year after NZR became aware of the PNG Chiefs name, was not appropriate.

He said an injunction now would cloud the franchise's reputation ahead of a recruitment blitz once free agency opens in November.

stories.headline: Who is this year's Mr. October? Tracking the playoff MVP for 2026
stories.summary: We go inside the numbers on the players doing the most to help their teams win.
stories.body:
Who is hero of the 2026 MLB playoffs?

To try to answer to that question, we're tabulating the cumulative win probability added figures for every player in the postseason. But we've added a twist: The deeper we get into the playoffs, the more weight the WPA carries. The division series counts double the wild-card round, then we'll double it again for the championship series and, finally, once again for the World Series.

This means that players who shine in the early rounds can still get on the leaderboard, but it's more difficult. Coming through when the championship leverage is at its highest is what becoming an October hero is all about.

Thursday's hero: Aaron Ashby was already our HeroAXE leader before Thursday's games. Then he went out and threw three scoreless innings to slam the door on the Dodgers and clinch Milwaukee's first pennant in 44 years. Not a bad night's work. Ashby has now appeared in six postseason games during which he's earned a win, two saves and a hold. He has not allowed a run in 12 ⅓ innings and has surrendered a .329 OPS. Could Ashby really garner some real-world consideration for playoff MVP? If the playoffs were over now, you could really make that argument.

Methodology
As mentioned above, each player's win probability added (WPA) is tracked on a per-game basis. Each round of the playoffs counts double that of the previous round. The tabulation is then converted to an AXE-style index in which 100 represents the average for all postseason players. The "Change" column looks in the changes in AXE numbers from the previous day for players who were in action. You can sort this column by clicking on it to see the day's heroes.

stories.headline: Alone on a fantasy basketball island: 'One player I feel differently about'
stories.summary: The fantasy basketball crew identifies one player they feel differently about than seemingly everyone else.
stories.body:
With how closely fantasy basketball managers and analysts are watching every player and roster role, it's easy get lost in all of the information available. But beyond that, everyone has that one opinion they may be a little stubborn on.

You know, that one player you are certain will break out to join the league's elite. Or maybe a player everyone around is high on, but you're feeling the "meh."

That's why we asked our fantasy basketball experts André Snellings, Eric Moody, Eric Karabell, Jim McCormick, Michael F. Florio and Steve Alexander to identify a player they feel differently about for this season and their bold prediction why.

See more: Sign up | Rankings | Projections | Mock Draft Lobby

Draft guide | Cheat sheet | Which league is right for you?

Fred VanVleet is a steal at his current spot

VanVleet going outside the top 100 picks is one of the easiest clicks of the draft button for me. I understand that he missed last season, but any risk is already baked into his ADP. He's back as the starting point guard for a very talented Rockets team. VanVleet is a season removed from averaging eight assists per game. He averaged over 17 fantasy PPG in five of his last six seasons. You can take Desmond Bane in the top 50 picks, or wait and get similar production with VanVleet. -- Florio

LaMelo Ball could have the best season of his career

I am higher than most on LaMelo Ball. Ball played in 72 games last season, his most since the 2021-22 campaign, but he also played a career-low 28.0 MPG with associated lesser volume. But in the three previous, injury-shortened seasons, Ball averaged much higher volume at 24.1 PPG, 7.9 APG and 5.5 RPG. With Ball moving to the Timberwolves, a team that has desperately needed a playmaker, and playing as one of two elite offensive options next to Anthony Edwards, I could see Ball having the best season of his career. I remember Ball was a preseason top-10 player entering the 2022-23 campaign before the ankle injuries slowed him down, and if he stays healthy I could see him return to that range this season. -- Snellings

Jaren Jackson Jr.'s days as a top-100 option could be over

After years of investing in JJJ, I am out, especially in points formats. Jackson blocks shots and shoots well, but we cannot count on Jackson averaging 20 PPG again, and he has never been much of a rebounder or passer, routinely piling on more turnovers than assists. Considering his size and talent, there is no reason for Jackson to average fewer than eight RPG. He's not even getting six RPG! Darryn Peterson and Ace Bailey are Utah's future. Jackson's role may be reduced even further, enough that he may no longer be a top-100 fantasy option at all. -- Karabell

Take Kyrie Irving in the fourth or fifth round

I seem to be of a different mindset on Kyrie Irving, who hasn't played meaningful basketball since March of 2025. But he looks healthy to me, is nearly guaranteed to have second-round value if he can stay healthy, and might be the best point guard value-pick in the draft. I like drafting him in Round 4 or Round 5 and cannot wait to watch him play a full season with Cooper Flagg. Irving has the best handle, is an offensive force and should be an excellent source of point guard numbers in fantasy. I don't see how he doesn't at least hit value and I'm all in. -- Alexander

Brandon Miller could make the leap to stardom

While there is some growing optimism around Brandon Miller and his potential to grow in the wake of LaMelo Ball's departure, more on-ball work, initiating and curating the offense for Charlotte could result in career bests across the board for this ascendant wing. I am willing to draft Miller well above his current draft position (59th in ESPN ADP) given his real candidacy to lead the league in 3-point volume. Growth isn't linear, as this could be an exponential leap to prime Paul George production from Miller. -- McCormick

Darius Garland has top-30 potential

I'm all in on Garland. Kawhi Leonard is gone, Brandon Ingram is sidelined, so Garland should be the focal point of the Clippers' offense. He averaged 19.9 PPG, 6.4 APG and 1.2 SPG in 19 games with the Clippers last season despite battling toe injuries. Now healthy, Garland has a chance to return to the form that saw him average 21.7 PPG and 8.6 APG in 2021-22. His usage should be among the highest of his career, and at his average draft position, I wouldn't be surprised if Garland finishes inside the top 30. -- Moody

stories.headline: Arsenal's Mikel Arteta defends Viktor Gyökeres after goalless start to season
stories.summary: Mikel Arteta has defended Viktor Gyökeres amid criticism of the Arsenal striker's start to the season.
stories.body:
Mikel Arteta has defended Viktor Gyökeres amid criticism of the Arsenal striker's start to the season.

Gyökeres arrived last summer in a €73 million (£61.5m) deal from Sporting CP and scored 14 Premier League goals as the Gunners won the title for the first time in 22 years.

However, Arsenal spent the summer scouring the market for another attacking option with Atletico Madrid's Julián Álvarez among their leading targets with reports in Spain suggesting Gyokeres could have been used as a makeweight in a potential deal.

Arsenal were unable to prise Alvarez away from Madrid and opted not to sign a forward with Arteta preferring Kai Havertz to Gyökeres in the club's biggest games so far this season.

Gyökeres is yet to score in seven appearances this term but Arteta believes that was close to changing in his 65-minute display against Lille on Tuesday night.

Speaking on Friday ahead of the weekend trip to Nottingham Forest, Arteta said: "These are moments in a player's career, or in a season I would say. We are trying to help him as much as possible.

"The other day, he had some very good moments. He was three or four times in front of goal with no keeper, the ball should arrive to him and it doesn't and maybe you are talking about something else.

"But these are the strikers. It is very small margins. Scoring or not scoring changes the narrative, for sure not the perception how much he can help the team."

Gyökeres had just 12 touches and failed to register a shot against Lille.

- Arsenal's Mikel Merino: I am 'fortunate to be alive' after Dortmund bus attack

- Arsenal's Eberechi Eze to perform Cristiano Ronaldo-inspired celebration after loss to IShowSpeed

Havertz is expected to return to the starting line-up at the City Ground and when asked whether Gyökeres is suffering from a lack of confidence, Arteta said: "That's a very person question. What he transmits is an incredible will and determination and work rate to improve and help the team.

"That's Viktor every single day regardless of his position, whether he scored a goal or not. And that's why he's always an option to play."

Arteta confirmed Piero Hincapié is still "a week or two" away from returning to action following an ankle injury while Martín Zubimendi [also ankle] is progressing well and could be available within the next week.

stories.headline: NHL Power Rankings: Each team's biggest shock of 2026-27
stories.summary: The Hurricanes are back on top of our 1-32 poll. Plus, we identify the big surprises -- both good and bad.
stories.body:
A bit over two weeks into the 2026-27 NHL season, teams are approaching the 10-game point.

While some teams have performed at expectation, there has been no shortage of surprises -- both good and bad -- on the individual and club-wide level.

So as part of our latest update to the ESPN NHL Power Rankings, we've identified the biggest shock of the season for each team.

How we rank: A panel of ESPN hockey commentators, analysts, reporters and editors sends in a 1-32 poll based on the games through Wednesday. Those ballots are combined to come up with the rankings you see below.

Note: Previous ranking for each team refers to the previous edition, published on Oct. 9. Points percentages are through Thursday's games.

1. Carolina Hurricanes
Previous ranking: 8

Points percentage: 81.25%

While the Canes' spot near the top of the standings (and as the No. 1 team here) isn't too surprising, their poor injury luck is. In just the past week, captain Jordan Staal (torn calf muscle) and Taylor Hall (upper body) were lost; Staal will miss one to two months, while Rod Brind'Amour commented that it "doesn't look good" for Hall.

Next seven days: @ WPG (Oct. 17), @ CGY (Oct. 18), @ VAN (Oct. 20), @ EDM (Oct. 22)

2. Vegas Golden Knights
Previous ranking: 3

Points percentage: 77.78%

The Golden Knights continue to roll on the ice -- but there are now fewer people in the stands watching. Oct. 8 was the first time the Knights didn't sell out a home game in franchise history, breaking a nine-year streak (and coming off a Stanley Cup Final appearance).

Next seven days: vs. PIT (Oct. 17), vs. TB (Oct. 20), @ STL (Oct. 22)

3. Edmonton Oilers
Previous ranking: 6

Points percentage: 78.57%

It's no surprise that Connor McDavid and Leon Draisaitl are among the top scorers in the league. What might be shocking to some is that defenseman Evan Bouchard is right there as well, as he had 14 points through the first six games. That's on pace for 196 at season's end!

Next seven days: @ UTA (Oct. 17), vs. MIN (Oct. 20), vs. CAR (Oct. 22)

4. Utah Mammoth
Previous ranking: 2

Points percentage: 75%

Following a playoff appearance this past spring, the Mammoth have been a wagon to start the campaign. Led by Clayton Keller, Nick Schmaltz and Mikhail Sergachev, the Mammoth are scoring 3.88 goals per game, more than half a goal more per contest than last season.

Next seven days: vs. EDM (Oct. 17), vs. PIT (Oct. 19), @ SEA (Oct. 22)

5. New York Rangers
Previous ranking: 5

Points percentage: 66.67%

The Rangers' hot start may have been surprising to some, but the season-ending injury to goaltender Igor Shesterkin is clearly a bigger shock. That's put Dylan Garand in the spotlight, and he's been a pleasant surprise himself (up until Thursday's misstep against the rival Devils).

Next seven days: @ CBJ (Oct. 17), vs. ANA (Oct. 19), @ TOR (Oct. 22)

6. Colorado Avalanche
Previous ranking: 1

Points percentage: 64.29%

The Avs look every bit the part of a top Cup contender, as expected. What wasn't expected? That Nathan MacKinnon would already have two fights under his belt in the season's first two weeks.

Next seven days: vs. PIT (Oct. 16), @ PHI (Oct. 19), @ NJ (Oct. 20)

7. Boston Bruins
Previous ranking: 19

Points percentage: 71.43%

The Bruins are trending well ahead of their expected point total, and a big reason why is Fraser Minten. The 22-year-old is scoring at a point-per-game pace after just 35 in 82 games in 2025-26.

Next seven days: @ ANA (Oct. 16), @ LA (Oct. 17), @ DAL (Oct. 20), vs. NSH (Oct. 22)

8. Minnesota Wild
Previous ranking: 4

Points percentage: 68.75%

Perhaps we shouldn't be all that surprised given the chatter during the summer, but it is a bit of a shock that the Wild have begun the season with Quinn Hughes on an expiring contract. Unsurprisingly, Hughes is battling with Kirill Kaprizov for the team scoring lead -- the winger currently has a slight edge on the defenseman.

Next seven days: vs. CBJ (Oct. 18), @ EDM (Oct. 20)

9. Tampa Bay Lightning
Previous ranking: 10

Points percentage: 71.43%

Andrei Vasilevskiy and the goal suppressors in Tampa continue to do their jobs; the Lightning are allowing 2.67 goals per game through six contests, about on par with last season. The goal scoring is lagging, however: the Lightning's 2.83 goals per contest are 21st in the NHL and a far cry from the 3.49 per game rate of last season.

Next seven days: vs. VAN (Oct. 17), @ VGK (Oct. 20)

10. Seattle Kraken
Previous ranking: 16

Points percentage: 68.75%

Short-sample warning and all, but ... are the Kraken good? A 5-2-1 record has them among the Pacific Division leaders, and a plus-9 goal differential indicates that it's not all smoke and mirrors.

Next seven days: @ FLA (Oct. 17), vs. DET (Oct. 20), vs. UTA (Oct. 22)

11. Winnipeg Jets
Previous ranking: 12

Points percentage: 71.43%

If the Jets were going to contend amid the ongoing Connor Hellebuyck trade request fiasco, their stars would need to shine the brightest. Kyle Connor understood the assignment, beginning the season with a shocking seven goals through six games.

Next seven days: vs. CAR (Oct. 17), @ STL (Oct. 20), @ DAL (Oct. 22)

12. Ottawa Senators
Previous ranking: 13

Points percentage: 75%

With Brady Tkachuk in the lineup last season, the Senators were a wild-card team. Without him this season, they're ... more dangerous? Netminder Linus Ullmark posting a 1.20 goals-against average and .949 save percentage through six starts (all wins) is the type of pleasant surprise that drives success like Ottawa's.

Next seven days: @ PHI (Oct. 17), vs. FLA (Oct. 21), vs. SJ (Oct. 22)

13. Florida Panthers
Previous ranking: 7

Points percentage: 62.5%

Was there something in the air on opening night in Raleigh? Just like the Hurricanes, the Panthers have been beset by a shocking string of injuries to key players, principally Aleksander Barkov and Brad Marchand.

Next seven days: vs. SEA (Oct. 17), @ OTT (Oct. 21), @ PIT (Oct. 22)

14. Anaheim Ducks
Previous ranking: 9

Points percentage: 66.67%

It has been an up-and-down start for the Ducks after their impressive flight in 2025-26. But one area that has been a nice surprise is the power play: Their man-advantage unit is clicking along at 33.3% through six games, up from 18.6% last season.

Next seven days: vs. BOS (Oct. 16), @ NYR (Oct. 19), @ NYI (Oct. 20), @ NJ (Oct. 22)

15. Washington Capitals
Previous ranking: 15

Points percentage: 57.14%

The Capitals' front office did a nice job making additions this summer, including Alex Tuch. The former Sabre leads the team with five goals through seven games; that's on pace for 60, which would shatter his career high of 36.

Next seven days: vs. NJ (Oct. 17), vs. LA (Oct. 20)

16. St. Louis Blues
Previous ranking: 28

Points percentage: 50%

Perhaps this will only surprise those who weren't paying close attention to the Blues last season, but Joel Hofer has emerged not only as the Blues' best option in the crease, but as an upper-echelon netminder leaguewide, with a 1.76 goals-against average and .920 save percentage through four starts.

Next seven days: @ NSH (Oct. 17), vs. WPG (Oct. 20), vs. VGK (Oct. 22)

17. Dallas Stars
Previous ranking: 17

Points percentage: 50%

After having the NHL's second-best power play last season (28.6%), the Stars have struggled there this season, converting at a 12.5% rate through seven games.

Next seven days: @ CHI (Oct. 17), vs. BOS (Oct. 20), vs. WPG (Oct. 22)

18. Pittsburgh Penguins
Previous ranking: 11

Points percentage: 50%

Typically, Sidney Crosby gets out to quick starts: Up through last season, he scored 1.2 points per game in the first month during his career. Through seven games, he has just four points (0.57 points per game). Something tells us he'll turn things around soon.

Next seven days: @ COL (Oct. 16), @ VGK (Oct. 17), @ UTA (Oct. 19), vs. FLA (Oct. 22)

19. Toronto Maple Leafs
Previous ranking: 21

Points percentage: 50%

Following a disappointing 2025-26, there was some chatter that captain Auston Matthews wanted out. Instead, he and William Nylander have both been on a tear to start the season, with 12 points apiece through seven games.

Next seven days: vs. NYI (Oct. 17), vs. SJ (Oct. 19), @ CBJ (Oct. 20), vs. NYR (Oct. 22)

20. Buffalo Sabres
Previous ranking: 14

Points percentage: 56.25%

A goals-per-game rate of 3.45 last season brought about major success for the Sabres: the first playoff appearance since 2011, and a whole slew of new fans. Unfortunately, that scoring has dried up considerably in the opening weeks of 2026-27, with just 3.00 goals per contest through eight of them.

Next seven days: @ MTL (Oct. 17), vs. PHI (Oct. 21)

21. Montreal Canadiens
Previous ranking: 20

Points percentage: 50%

Goaltender Jakub Dobes was a major part of the Canadiens' run to the 2026 Eastern Conference finals -- and a big reason why many prognosticators had the Habs taking another step forward this season. Unfortunately, Dobes has had difficulty at launch this season, with a 4.63 goals-against average and .841 save percentage through four starts.

Next seven days: vs. BUF (Oct. 17), vs. SJ (Oct. 20)

22. New York Islanders
Previous ranking: 23

Points percentage: 50%

Some scoffed at the idea that Isles sophomore D-man Matthew Schaefer was worthy of the No. 16 in the ESPN NHL Top 100 this season. But after a unanimous Calder Trophy win last year, he's scoring at a point-per-game pace this season.

Next seven days: @ TOR (Oct. 17), vs. ANA (Oct. 20), vs. LA (Oct. 22)

23. New Jersey Devils
Previous ranking: 27

Points percentage: 57.14%

Overall expectations have gone unmet for the Devils this season, and part of it is a penalty kill that is lagging behind last season's edition. Killing just 71.4% of penalties thus far, that's good for 26th in the NHL, a meaningful drop from killing 79.3% of them last season (17th).

Next seven days: @ WSH (Oct. 17), vs. COL (Oct. 20), vs. ANA (Oct. 22)

24. San Jose Sharks
